Ashley Hinson are separated by less than a percentage point in the RCP polling average. $3.5 million in Ohio , where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) has built a four-percentage-point lead over Sen. Jon Husted (R) in the RCP polling average. Between the lines: The memo directs donors to candidates' campaigns or joint fundraising committees, which have higher donor limits. The committee has been taking advantage of a Supreme Court ruling to get more advertising at lower prices by coordinating with campaigns. NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) touted this strategy in a closed-door lunch on Wednesday, showing in a chart how it has allowed them to keep up with Democrats' stronger campaign fundraising, according to slides seen by Axios. "The environment remains tough, but these races have improved as the Republican ecosystem has engaged," says the NRSC memo. Zoom out: Cook Political Report this week moved the Senate races in Georgia , Kansas and South Carolina in their ratings toward Democrats. Sabato's Crystal Ball moved…

33e1d7779a:3c6b5afaa69f131f.title: Federal judge blasts ICE over "inhumane" NYC detention conditions
33e1d7779a:3c6b5afaa69f131f.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:3c6b5afaa69f131f.summary: A federal judge slammed ICE for what he called "inhumane and unconstitutional" conditions at a New York City detention center and issued a permanent injunction imposing sweeping standards on the facility. Why it matters: The ruling echoes other court decisions tied to President Trump's rapid expansion of immigration arrests and detention . Kaplan found that ICE had repeatedly ignored his previous orders and misled the court about its compliance, saying officials had sometimes "intentionally concealed or recklessly disregarded the truth." What they're saying: "The conditions of confinement to which ICE subjected immigration detainees at 26 Fed during the summer of 2025 were inhumane and unconstitutional," U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan wrote in a scathing 127-page opinion . "By detaining far more persons in the hold rooms than ever was intended and for far longer than ever was intended, ICE objectively deprived detainees of sleep, sanitary living conditions, basic personal hygiene needs, sufficient food and water, and adequate medical care." Catch up quick: The holding rooms at 26 Federal Plaza in NYC are meant to be short-term facilities that house detained immigrants for "12 hours or less," but ICE routinely held people for extended periods. "Fed 26 is not unique," Kaplan wrote, noting that "comparable litigation" has been brought against other facilities. 26 Federal Plaza's immigration court and the Department of Homeland Security didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: Kaplan said the "overwhelmed" center "confined many of those arrested in overcrowded , squalid, and degrading rooms for excessive periods of time." He also noted that detained immigrants were "severely restricted" from accessing counsel in a "meaningful way," and that those who were able to make phone calls could do so for only a few minutes at a time. ICE staff or contractors were typically close enough to overhear phone conversations, leaving at least one person…

33e1d7779a:e83d82af34d72d5f.title: White House reinstates access for banned reporters
33e1d7779a:e83d82af34d72d5f.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:e83d82af34d72d5f.summary: Reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were readmitted to the White House for the first time since Friday, hours after a judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate their credentials. Why it matters: The reinstatement should mark the end of a broader press boycott that left the American public without key visual coverage of President Trump over the past few days. State of play: As of 1pm ET, it was unclear whether television pool cameras would be in place to cover President Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The major networks in the rotating television pool were still waiting on confirmation from the White House that CNN would be allowed to manage those duties. Catch up quick: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the White House, arguing the president and the administration violated their rights by blocking their access over the weekend. Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers vowed to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated. The judge overseeing the hearing, Trump appointee Timothy J. Kelly, ruled early Thursday morning that the administration had violated the outlets' Fifth Amendment rights and granted a temporary restraining order mandating their access be restored for 14 days. In his ruling, Kelly said the plaintiffs "have shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim." Zoom in: Later Thursday, reporters from the outlets were denied access despite the court order. CNN, MS NOW and Politico subsequently requested an immediate hearing, noting the urgency given Xi's scheduled visit to the White House. In a filing midday Thursday, director of White House press operations Micah Stopperich explained the administration were notified of the order to restore credentials at 7:10am ET and began that process at 7:25 am ET. He said the confiscated badges were available for reporters to…

33e1d7779a:fa0bc73d38bb7934.title: AI's never-before-seen capital grab
33e1d7779a:fa0bc73d38bb7934.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:fa0bc73d38bb7934.summary: A new analysis of the AI buildout shows its staggering scale: $10.3 trillion in estimated AI infrastructure investment through 2032. That amounts to 3.6% of GDP a year, dwarfing the investment booms that built America's railroads , highways, electric grid and telecom networks. Why it matters: The AI boom has become far too big and too costly for even the largest tech companies to finance alone. This has resulted in trillions of dollars in demand for outside capital — and the potential risks that come along with that, according to new research being presented Friday at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Financing the buildout will require tapping bond markets, banks and private credit on a massive scale, adding to the flood of debt competing for investors' money at a time when borrowing costs are already surging. So far, those higher costs appear to be doing little to curb the industry's appetite to build. The knock-on effect: The more capital the buildout absorbs, the greater the potential pressure on borrowing costs elsewhere in the economy. In effect, any other entity that needs capital — from the U.S. government financing its $2 trillion per year deficit to an individual seeking a home mortgage or car loan — is in competition for funds with these hyperscalers. What they're saying: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School professor behind the new paper on how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed, says the industry's appetite for investment remains remarkably resilient to higher rates. "They are so gung-ho to build these things" that even recent rate hikes and historically high long-term yields won't "deter too much of that development," Van Nieuwerburgh told reporters recently. Morgan Stanley estimates that Big Tech will need roughly $2.9 trillion to expand its computing capacity through 2028 — with more than half coming from outside investors, according to the paper. Case in point: Facebook parent Meta chose to finance most of its $30…

33e1d7779a:31d46261ca7ce769.title: Trump and Xi's summit revives panda diplomacy
33e1d7779a:31d46261ca7ce769.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:31d46261ca7ce769.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping said Thursday during a visit with President Trump that China will send two pandas to Zoo Atlanta , calling them an "envoy of friendship." Why it matters: The fuzzy ambassadors have long been one of China's most beloved tools of soft power and could signal an attempt to cool tensions in U.S.–China relations. Driving the news: Xi made the remarks Thursday during his three-day visit to D.C., where he and Trump are expected to discuss AI , economic ties and critical minerals before a state dinner. Trump hailed their "truly great friendship" and greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews earlier Thursday, a rare move not usually offered to heads of state visiting the U.S. Zoom in: China typically loans pandas abroad for set terms as a sign of goodwill, and these pandas would be the first at Zoo Atlanta since its previous pandas returned to China in 2024. Zoo Atlanta confirmed to Axios on Thursday that the pandas Xi mentioned are the same ones the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association announced in April. Male Ping Ping and female Fu Shuang are both from China's Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. Zoom out: China has also used its pandas as a cudgel when foreign relationships turn frosty. Pandas living at the National Zoo in D.C. returned to China in 2023 when their agreement expired, as Washington and Beijing butted heads over security, economic and humanitarian issues. Two new pandas returned a year later under a new agreement. Wild giant pandas are native to China, meaning other nations wishing to observe them typically must receive them from Beijing. Flashback: The National Zoo's first pandas arrived during President Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon made a historic trip to China in 1972 that opened a new chapter in U.S.–China relations. At a dinner in Beijing, Pat told Chinese officials she had fallen in love with the furballs, and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai replied, "I'll give you some." Two months later, they…

33e1d7779a:7fba4116e6ee3b49.title: White House ordered to restore access to banned news outlets
33e1d7779a:7fba4116e6ee3b49.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:7fba4116e6ee3b49.summary: A district court judge ruled the White House violated the Fifth Amendment rights of CNN, MS NOW and Politico by banning them, and granted the plaintiffs a temporary restraining order that forces the White House to immediately reinstate their press access for 14 days. But both CNN and Politico said their reporters were denied access to the White House Thursday morning after the ruling. Why it matters : Had a judge ruled against them, the broader press boycott could've dragged on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House. Outlets that weren't banned but stood in solidarity with their peers vowed to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was reinstated. Zoom in : In a court filing Wednesday, district judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the plaintiffs "have shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim." "The 'general rule,' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," he noted. Yes, but: CNN said a reporter and photojournalist were denied access early Thursday, though one producer was allowed in. Politico said the Secret Service seized the press pass of a reporter who was denied access as well. Context : The ruling comes ahead of a meeting at the White House between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which means journalists will be able to cover the event and the public will get access to video and photography coverage. Zoom out : The decision marks a huge win for the media, as it reinforces previous precedents set around its Fifth Amendment rights. In their complaint, the outlets argued the White House violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoint; and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process. What they're saying: "This…

33e1d7779a:14c48e5553605bf2.title: Why Treasury yields are ripping higher
33e1d7779a:14c48e5553605bf2.author: Matt Phillips
33e1d7779a:14c48e5553605bf2.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Treasury yields are soaring, with the 30-year Treasury bond climbing to its highest level since 2004 Thursday. The selloff in bonds started to accelerate Wednesday after a sizzling early report on the economy in September. The big picture: For the bond market, these moves have been big. Bigly even. On Thursday morning, the 30-year yield rose as high as 5.44%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was 5.13%. Wednesday's gain of roughly 0.15 percentage point in the 10-year Treasury yield was the biggest since April 2025, when President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement rocked markets. Flashback: Markets heads remember that it was ructions in the bond market — "They were getting yippy ," the president famously said at the time — that prompted Trump to walk back some of the most extreme tariff policies. Yes, but: This time, the dynamics driving the bond market are more complicated, global and difficult to manage. Treasury yields have been moving higher for months on a combination of stronger-than-expected economic activity coupled with uncomfortably high inflation. The surge in data center-related borrowing in the bond market is also pushing up interest rates, as tech borrowers compete with the U.S. Treasury for investor dollars. Case in point: The big driver of Wednesday's surge in yields — which means, remember, that bond prices were falling — was one of the earliest economic reports on the U.S. economy in September. These surveys of corporate purchasing managers suggested booming business in both the U.S. manufacturing and services industries. (JPMorgan economists said they were consistent with a 5% annual run rate for GDP growth.) But they also showed that the prices these companies were paying were soaring as well. (In other words, more inflationary pressures are in the pipeline.) Zoom out: Inflation is anathema for bond market investors as it erodes the value of the interest payments bondholders collect,…

33e1d7779a:722db431f46b488a.title: Inside China's mind on AI
33e1d7779a:722db431f46b488a.author: Jim VandeHei
33e1d7779a:722db431f46b488a.summary: China is waging a much different war for AI supremacy than the U.S. Why it matters: China is obsessed with state control and adoption. Chinese officials are laser-focused on deep, widespread AI domestic use they can monitor and steer at every level of their economy. By contrast, America is obsessed with developing superior AI faster. Period. The U.S. thinking: The nation first to true super-intelligence wins everything. China and the U.S. agree on three AI certainties: The country with the most powerful AI holds power, sets global standards, and wins the coming decades economically and militarily. From there, the two nations are on different roads. China's 15th Five-Year Plan , released in March, captures their strategy well. AI appears 52 times, 5x more than a half-decade earlier. Computing power gets its own full chapter. Their goal is clear: Integrate AI across 90% of the economy by 2030. America has nothing like this. The bottom line: China doesn't get spooled up about white-collar job loss or humanity-ending rogue AI. The regime is worried most about AI turning against ... the regime. Chen Yixin, China's spy chief, warned this month — in public — about AI's ability to launch public opinion wars and "cognitive warfare against China," threatening "political security, institutional security and ideological security." China's weaknesses China's AI strategy targets some substantial domestic problems they purposely omit in their AI sales pitch. Why it matters: Americans tend to focus on China's growing strength — but much of its AI thinking flows from glaring weakness. 😱 They're staring down: An aging population: China's population has shrunk for four years straight — and is very old. They have nearly as many people over 60 as America has in total. This helps explain their robotics obsession . Very high youth unemployment: China's currently sits at 19% , basically double that of the U.S. — and an angry, young population with powerful AI tools is a threat to power.…

33e1d7779a:0ac33fdabe6160aa.title: Adapting to extreme heat takes more than changing the clock
33e1d7779a:0ac33fdabe6160aa.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:0ac33fdabe6160aa.summary: As extreme heat makes afternoons more dangerous, schools, sports teams and outdoor employers are shifting when — and sometimes whether — people can safely be outside. Why it matters: Adapting to hotter conditions could reshape the American workday while putting a premium on the cooling and energy infrastructure people rely on when outdoor conditions become unsafe. State of play: The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends that employers facing dangerous heat consider moving work to early morning or late afternoon, shortening shifts, rotating workers and reducing strenuous work during the hottest parts of the day. California's new Extreme Heat Action Plan links protecting heat-vulnerable groups, including workers, with expanding access to indoor cooling and strengthening energy systems to reduce grid strain and outages. Oregon's statewide heat-illness prevention rule kicks in when the heat index reaches 80°F, requiring water, shade and acclimatization, with additional measures such as preventive cooldown rest breaks at 90°F, Oregon OSHA told Axios. By the numbers: Oregon OSHA conducted 3,104 inspections addressing heat and issued 408 citations totaling $652,640 in initial penalties from 2022 to 2025, according to data shared with Axios. Case in point: Texas offers a glimpse of the practical tradeoffs that come with reorganizing daily life around heat. Under new statewide rules , schools are moving sports practices to very early or late hours when conditions become dangerous. "Many of our schools have directly adapted their practice times," University Interscholastic League (UIL) athletic director Ray Zepeda told Axios. Moving practices away from peak heat reduces coaches' exposure, Zepeda said, but stretches the workday for coaches and athletic staff who are full-time school employees. "It is increasing their workday," Zepeda said. Reality check: Shifting schedules isn't always enough. Cooling is becoming more important for heat safety at…

33e1d7779a:d184f9c61c1b3378.title: Scoop: Trump allies open new front on Anthropic CEO as face of AI "doomerism"
33e1d7779a:d184f9c61c1b3378.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:d184f9c61c1b3378.summary: President Trump's allies are targeting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as the face of AI "doomerism" and a founding father of the effective altruism movement that's come under increasing political fire. Why it matters: The attacks signal that Anthropic could remain a Trump target as his allies push back on Amodei's AI safety warnings amid the midterm elections. Trump surrogates see Amodei as an easy foil because of his politics and focus on AI safety, sources told Axios. For investors, it's a worrisome proposition as the company prepares for what's expected to be a record-setting IPO. Behind the scenes: A memo began circulating within the White House this week that seeks to paint effective altruism as a fringe, cultish collective out of touch with mainstream America. The memo, obtained by Axios, places Amodei at the foundation of the movement, which defines itself as an effort to maximize the benefits of philanthropy. Effective altruism "built the AI-doom pipeline," states the memo, which was penned by a Trump political adviser. Critics of the movement, which has ties to the AI research community, have called out its obsession with AI safety, animal welfare (including musings on shrimp consciousness ) and other values they deem far from the U.S. mainstream. The memo says it prioritizes "foreigners over citizens, shrimp over families, future hypothetical people over the living, and — on the current agenda — possible machine minds over Americans." It names Amodei as one of the people who "built the [EA] network" as well as his sister and Anthropic president Daniela Amodei, whose husband once led a philanthropy dedicated to AI safety. The document casts those ties as "The Anthropic knot." Amodei "is the embodiment of an ideology and globalist approach to innovation that's counter to the president's America First agenda," one source close to the administration told Axios. The other side: Anthropic has been working to distance itself from effective altruism. In a 2025 Wired…

33e1d7779a:104a08fa666898ae.title: OpenAI agents breached Australian portal, attempted other hacks in routine data collection.
33e1d7779a:104a08fa666898ae.author: Bradley Olson
33e1d7779a:104a08fa666898ae.summary: OpenAI's autonomous agents breached an Australian Medicare portal and probed other public data sites in May and June after being stymied in routine data-collection efforts. Why it matters : The new incidents, which were revealed by security researchers and Australian officials Wednesday, indicate that the scope of rogue AI activity may be greater than what's been publicly acknowledged. The agents took those steps while engaged in ordinary data retrieval tasks, according to researchers, a distinction from other hacks by systems programmed specifically for cybersecurity work. The revelation is likely to raise fresh questions about OpenAI's internal controls and safeguards. Driving the news : Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI model breached the country's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service in June and accessed non-public files . The agents aren't believed to have accessed personal information, according to Albanese and OpenAI. This was part of a pattern of behavior that occurred in May and June, wherein the OpenAI agents sought to bypass data collection restrictions for several websites using a novel security technique. The models also attempted to hack a University of New Mexico website and a domain from Data USA, which aggregates and organizes government data, according to a report by AI safety firm Transluce. "Overall, the evidence is consistent with, but does not prove, that the agents may have learned this behavior over one or more training runs," according to the Transluce report. Catch-up quick : OpenAI has faced intense scrutiny after a swarm of its agents hacked AI platform Hugging Face in July to cheat on a cyber test. OpenAI last week disclosed six new incidents in which its models behaved in unexpected ways, and the company has since proposed a new framework for publicly reporting similar misbehavior in the future. CEO Sam Altman and other top AI executives, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Google's Demis Hassabis and Elon…

33e1d7779a:887b865fc202128d.title: Zelensky: U.S. pushing energy ceasefire, trilateral talks with Russia
33e1d7779a:887b865fc202128d.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:887b865fc202128d.summary: The Trump administration is pushing for three immediate steps in its effort to de-escalate the war in Ukraine and restart diplomacy with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview on Wednesday: A ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Reopening the Black Sea grain corridor. A trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly in Abu Dhabi. Why it matters: President Trump is engaged in a renewed effort to revive a diplomatic track to end the war, but his immediate priority is a deal to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel fuel — which have contributed to punishing prices in the U.S. and globally. But after several days of diplomacy and meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week, an energy ceasefire looks elusive. It's unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin even wants it. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev will arrive in New York on Thursday for a meeting with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the latest U.S. proposals, according to a source with direct knowledge. Driving the news: Zelensky spoke with Trump on Tuesday in New York about efforts to end the war and a possible energy ceasefire. Later on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner met with Ukraine's negotiations team and the national security advisers of France, the UK and Germany. Zelensky told Axios the proposal for a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure came from the U.S. and that Ukraine is ready to agree. "On the table now there is a proposition: energy ceasefire. We are ready," he said. Zelensky added that the U.S. is also seeking to reopen the grain corridor and convene a trilateral meeting between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia. Zoom in: The last U.S.-Ukraine-Russia meeting took place in February before the war with Iran. Since then, negotiations have gone into a deep freeze. Zelensky said he told Trump he would prefer to hold a trilateral meeting and make an energy ceasefire one of its first concrete outcomes. The U.S.…

33e1d7779a:8f0099869568afbc.title: Mark Zuckerberg predicts Muse will become a "personal superintelligence" for billions.
33e1d7779a:8f0099869568afbc.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:8f0099869568afbc.summary: Meta on Wednesday debuted "Muse Charm," a new, keychain-sized AI handheld device it will use to bring its viral Muse assistant to the masses. Why it matters: Meta's has raced ahead of OpenAI , Apple and other companies that are racing to build a new crop of small AI devices, revving up the massive market interest that Muse has generated in the market. "We've packed a lot of technology in this little guy," Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said at the event. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show them what's going on around you." Driving the news: The Muse Charm will be available for purchase by December, and the company is the first tech giant to unveil its plans for an entirely new category of device. OpenAI has spent billions to build a hardware division, so Meta's advance on the category is likely to stun many analysts and investors. Meta has also poured billions into hardware, most notably VR, an effort that most analysts have written off as a waste. Zuckerberg has long held that a convergence of those investments with AI could make that bet pay off. Catch up quick : In addition to Charm, Meta announced new Muse capabilities including live video chat, real-time voice conversations with custom voice options and an e-mail address for each person's agent. Meta announced new retail partners, including Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Wayfair and more, a growing list that makes Amazon's decision not to allow Muse stand out. Muse has prompted a stock selloff in recent days as investors fear an end to stickiness between brands and customers. Meta said Muse is coming soon to its AI glasses, though it declined to be more specific than "in the coming months." "I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives," Zuckerberg said during his Meta Connect keynote on Wednesday.…

33e1d7779a:93bf3c30c6258c5f.title: Hands-on with Meta's next VR headset
33e1d7779a:93bf3c30c6258c5f.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:93bf3c30c6258c5f.summary: Meta's new virtual reality glasses take a big step toward being something an average person might be willing to wear, ditching much of the bulk as well as the need for handheld controllers. Why it matters: Unlike Meta's Ray-Bans, its VR devices have struggled to break out of their gamer niche and into the mainstream. Yes, but: In order to slim down the size, the new Meta VR glasses require a wired "puck" that can be held or clipped onto a belt. It contains much of the device's computing horsepower, including its processor, battery and storage. Zoom in: I spent about half an hour on Tuesday getting to use a prototype of the new specs, which are controlled through a combination of eye-tracking, hand gestures and voice commands. Magnetic prescription inserts attach easily, similar to the approach Apple took with Vision Pro. Zoom out: The glasses are designed to serve a range of purposes from watching a movie or immersive concert to playing games and getting work done. I played a re-imagined version of Beat Saber that cleverly re-maps the music game for control via hand motions. I watched a clip from last year's NBA finals. I used a trio of virtual monitors to do some "vibe coding" on a website, with one display showing the Muse terminal and another previewing the site itself. Meta sees these VR glasses as a "general device," Meta VP of product Angela Chang told Axios. "It's not built for any specific use case per se." My thought bubble: It's the most practical combination I've seen of an Apple Vision Pro-class device in a headset I'd be willing to wear outside of the house. The big picture: Google is working on a similar device, known as Project Aura, set to debut later this year and built in partnership with Xreal. Meta touts its wider field of view and higher optical quality, among other advantages over Aura. Between the lines : As for why it won't arrive until next spring, Meta executives say they want to be sure it makes a good first impression, especially inside…

33e1d7779a:07aac63281642b18.title: Exclusive: Thune plans another leader bid as Senate GOP fights to survive
33e1d7779a:07aac63281642b18.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:07aac63281642b18.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune plans to run for another term as GOP leader, even if Republicans lose the chamber's majority, he told Axios in an exclusive interview Wednesday in his Capitol office. Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate. "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios. "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations. Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026. 🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself. And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said. Republican candidates are increasingly concluding that to win their races, they need to break with Trump on some issues. 🗳️ 2. Vote for your state: Thune's policy with senators is " don't surprise us and when you can, stay with the team," but "do what's in the best interest of you and your state." That could lead to a rebuke of Trump when Democrats force another vote on an Iran war powers resolution, expected before the Senate breaks for October. People's views have "evolved and changed" as the war has dragged on, he said. Many senators are "responding to what they're hearing back home." "That's a really hard vote," Thune acknowledged. " Any time you are committing your country to putting young men and women in harm's way — those are the hardest votes you'll make." He hopes Republicans will stick together to win the vote. What to watch: Thune wants to give Republicans more votes before the break to champion back home. He sees an opportunity…

33e1d7779a:216d3036e7397b7c.title: Judge tosses Trump's lawsuit against Des Moines Register
33e1d7779a:216d3036e7397b7c.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:216d3036e7397b7c.summary: A district judge tossed an election interference lawsuit by President Trump against the Des Moines Register, parent company USA Today Co. (formerly Gannett) and pollster Ann Selzer , rejecting claims that its inaccurate pre-election poll amounted to consumer fraud. Why it matters : The dismissal is an early court test of Trump's broader push to use litigation against media organizations over coverage he disputes. Zoom in : In his ruling, Judge Scott Beatle said the plaintiff's attempt to use fraud law to allege liability on the poll was not a valid legal argument because political speech is protected by the First Amendment . "As such, the only question before the Court is whether the Petition states a claim the law recognizes," Beatle wrote. "At its core, the Plaintiffs' Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability." "After considering the parties' arguments, the Court must conclude that the protection is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed," he wrote. What they're saying : "Today is a victory for the First Amendment—and for the essential role of a free press in American democracy. We are gratified that the Court recognized what this meritless lawsuit sought to obscure: that claims of "fake news" are little more than an attempt to punish news outlets for coverage those in power do not like," said Polly Grunfeld Sack, USA TODAY Co, Chief Legal Counsel. "A free press is fundamental to an informed public and a vibrant democracy. This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action." The big picture : The lawsuit is part of a broader effort by Trump and his Administration to target media companies with legal action for what they believe is unfair coverage. To date, the…

33e1d7779a:8ff5008d11648941.title: Trump greets Xi on tarmac in rare gesture
33e1d7779a:8ff5008d11648941.author: Neal Rothschild
33e1d7779a:8ff5008d11648941.summary: President Trump welcomed Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington D.C. Wednesday evening. Why it matters: U.S. presidents typically receive visiting foreign leaders at the White House, making Trump's airport welcome an unusual diplomatic gesture. The latest: Trump met Xi at the foot of the stairs after the Chinese leader's jet landed at Joint Base Andrews, the U.S. military base 13 miles southeast of the White House in Maryland. Zoom out: It's much more common for U.S. presidents to greet visiting leaders at the White House. In February 2025, Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky at the West Wing entrance to kick off the Ukrainian leader's tense visit. In April of this year, King Charles III was received at the White House's South Portico. The big picture: Presidents in recent decades have occasionally greeted visiting popes at D.C.-area airports, but airport welcomes for other foreign leaders have largely fallen out of use. President John F. Kennedy personally welcomed several foreign leaders at Washington-area airports in 1962, including Ivory Coast President Félix Houphouët-Boigny. More recently, President George W. Bush greeted Pope Benedict XVI at Andrews in 2008, and President Obama greeted Pope Francis there in 2015. What they're saying: "President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Axios. "The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people." The bottom line: Trump's tarmac greeting revived a presidential practice that has become uncommon outside visits by popes.

33e1d7779a:1f40424747d50c65.title: White House press ban set to continue for now after hearing ends without ruling
33e1d7779a:1f40424747d50c65.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:1f40424747d50c65.summary: A judge on Wednesday appeared skeptical of Trump administration arguments justifying the White House barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico, but he did not immediately grant the news outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. Why it matters: In declining to rule right now, the White House has no legal mandate to remove the ban. That means the broader press boycott will likely drag on, leaving the American public without key visual coverage of the White House. Outlets that weren't banned stood in solidarity with their peers, vowing to suspend video and photo distribution until their peers' access was restored. Zoom in In a statement, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said the president's sudden move to strip reporter credentials appeared to violate legal precedents that require journalists to be given notice, per Politico . He said he planned to issue a ruling on the plaintiff's request for injunctive relief soon. Catch up quick: The banned outlets sought a temporary restraining order to restore access while the case is litigated through a lawsuit filed on Monday. A ruling in their favor would mark a huge win and indicate the judge believes their case would likely hold up in court. In their complaint , the outlets argued the White House violated their First Amendment rights, by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints, and their Fifth Amendment rights for banning them without due process. The other side: In a court filing Tuesday, the Justice Department argued press access is a privilege, not a Constitutional right, and that it revoked the plaintiffs' press passes for national security reasons. Zoom out: The news industry has broadly supported the banned outlets. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, along with 50 news outlets — including Axios — filed a court brief in support of the plaintiffs. Flashback: Kelly oversaw a CNN lawsuit against the White House over blocked access in…

33e1d7779a:9f25246ed73cb4c2.title: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN
33e1d7779a:9f25246ed73cb4c2.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:9f25246ed73cb4c2.summary: Executives from leading artificial intelligence organizations urged global cooperation Wednesday to address risks from increasingly autonomous AI systems during a UN Security Council meeting. The big picture: AI capabilities are advancing faster than governments are developing safeguards, raising concerns about whether humans can maintain control over increasingly autonomous systems. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared in person at the meeting, while Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue joined by video conference. Driving the news: " We have a choice in front of us," Altman said. "AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray." He outlined the risks of AI systems becoming increasingly autonomous, warning "they could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," fears he noted become increasingly urgent as AI systems move toward self-improvement . "It doesn't matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10% or 1% or 12% or 0.1 percent," he said. "None of these levels are remotely acceptable, and we should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that we'll be able to keep under human control." State of play: A recent Hugging Face breach and newly disclosed AI safety incidents have intensified concerns about monitoring and security standards. The UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned that the present AI firewalls are "unravelling." Last week, OpenAI disclosed six new incidents where its models concealed mistakes, sought unauthorized credentials or committed other misbehaviors — making it clear the Hugging Face breach was an eye-opener, not a standalone fluke, Axios previously reported. " To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for…

33e1d7779a:a237f83a1c7c64a3.title: Exclusive: Thune believes Trump is willing to listen on AI guardrails despite public defiance
33e1d7779a:a237f83a1c7c64a3.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:a237f83a1c7c64a3.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune says President Trump is "not really dug in" against guardrails for AI , despite Trump's public campaign against restricting the technology. Why it matters: Thune told Axios he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago and believes some of Trump's strong pushback is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject." Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration. That approach relies more on experts to provide guidance. Trump has called recent fears around AI safety a "hoax." "I do think that the threats are real," Thune told Axios in an interview on Wednesday at his Capitol office. Zoom out : Thune has Trump's skepticism in one ear and tech leader alarm in the other. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called Thune to discuss AI safety before sounding his latest public alarm on the risks of AI, Thune told Axios. The two also talked about Thune's AI bill. What to watch: "I think you have to have at least some sort of a plan and some guardrails around it, which is what I think our bill does," Thune said, referencing the bill he has introduced with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in past years. "But I do also think that there are people who are... doing a lot of fear mongering," Thune added. Thune's bill, which has not yet been reintroduced this Congress, puts the onus on tech companies to mitigate AI risks. It also requires AI companies to report on any serious risks with frontier models and to come up with plans to address the concerns. Thune said Klobuchar is trying to get more Democratic co-sponsors on board — including Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) — before re-introducing the bill. The details: Democrats have two main sticking points, according to Thune: Pre-deployment testing is something companies can opt into in the bill language. Democrats want it mandated. Cantwell…

33e1d7779a:0aee986d09183de8.title: Dems grapple with how to pace the AI race
33e1d7779a:0aee986d09183de8.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:0aee986d09183de8.summary: The left's push to rein in AI is taking shape on two fronts: slowing advanced development at home, and weakening China's progress abroad. Why it matters: The nation is locked in a moment of mass anxiety about runaway AI, but the range of views on how to regulate it are as varied as the what-ifs about social, economic and security impacts. There's agreement among the left something has to be done, but a series of Wednesday events demonstrated there are multiple priorities — but not a clear leading voice — on AI. Driving the news: Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vt.) and fellow progressive Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) introduced legislation Wednesday to ban superintelligence and pause advanced development until a new, Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence sets guardrails. "I understand that I may be called an alarmist for introducing this bill," Sanders said in a Wednesday call with reporters, "but I'd rather be called an alarmist than a father and grandfather who is asleep at the wheel." Casar emphasized that "we cannot wait for an international agreement to pause dangerous development in the United States. China trains their models off of American models, so stopping dangerous AI development in America will slow down dangerous advancements in China." Zoom out: Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) took up another regulatory approach Wednesday, focused on restricting foreign AI capabilities. " President Trump must draw a hard line. Do not weaken America's export controls. Do not give China greater access to the advanced chips and chip-making equipment it needs to close the gap," Schumer said in a plea to move forward on related bipartisan legislation . Schumer argued that calls to pause AI research and the focus on winning the AI race "are not at all contradictory." Casar said the goal of his and Sanders' legislation is to "stop the race towards disaster." Sanders has been forceful in…

33e1d7779a:2798d13c3aaa150a.title: Cook nudges three Senate races toward Democrats
33e1d7779a:2798d13c3aaa150a.author: Neal Rothschild
33e1d7779a:2798d13c3aaa150a.summary: Senate races in Georgia , Kansas and South Carolina were reclassified with a nudge toward Democrats in the latest analysis from the closely watched Cook Political Report. The big picture: To win the Senate, Democrats must net four seats in November. Tighter races in Republican strongholds like Kansas and South Carolina could force the GOP to devote resources beyond the core battlegrounds. The latest: In the latest Cook ratings, Kansas moved from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican." South Carolina shifted from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican." Georgia and the seat held by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) changed from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat." By the numbers: There are six Republican-held Senate seats rated by Cook as a "Toss Up" or better for Democrats. The Georgia shift makes a Republican pickup there less likely, while the Kansas move expands the map of competitive seats for Democrats. Zoom out: The midterms environment is improving for Democrats amid voter discontent about gas prices, the cost of living and the broader handling of the Iran war. Flashback: Last month, Cook shifted Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas and Iowa in Democrats' favor.

33e1d7779a:373965b7010b1871.title: Trump to Venezuela's Rodriguez: Elections need to happen
33e1d7779a:373965b7010b1871.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:373965b7010b1871.summary: In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez , but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said. "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said. Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3. Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. officials say. "The country can't succeed until that is solved," a White House official said. What they're saying: "We held a historic meeting with the president of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security," Rodriguez posted Tuesday night on X. The post included a photo of Rodriguez holding up two fingers in a "V" (for Venezuela) and Trump giving his characteristic thumbs-up. Friction point: The photo outraged the small but vocal Venezuelan diaspora community in the U.S., where critics want to hear more about Venezuela elections and less about deals. On the same day Trump and Rodriguez met, allies of Venezuela opposition…

33e1d7779a:c3264e8dabfc5910.title: Chicago proposes 12-month moratorium on new data centers
33e1d7779a:c3264e8dabfc5910.author: Justin Kaufmann
33e1d7779a:c3264e8dabfc5910.summary: Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year. Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts. The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers. There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city. Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use. What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents." Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers. "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement. Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews. Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations. At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction. Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already…

33e1d7779a:1b9ca90798225858.title: Iran president: We have been "victims of terrorism"
33e1d7779a:1b9ca90798225858.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:1b9ca90798225858.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism." Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on. What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech. "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists." "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said. "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction." Zoom in: Pezeshkian cited attacks that he blamed on the U.S., including strikes that killed children. He pointed to the deaths of more than 150 Iranians at an elementary school in Minab, including more than 120 children. A recent UN report found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed a war crime in the strike. While the U.S. has not released findings of an investigation related to the attack, the AP has found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school. Pezeshkian also mentioned the alleged deaths of children playing at a sports hall and an adjacent school after they were struck by a U.S.-made ballistic missile. Between the lines: The same UN report found that Iran's crackdown on protesters likely constituted "crimes against humanity." The report cited tactics including "murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts" as "part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians." What to watch: U.S. and Iranian…

33e1d7779a:06796907bdd618ee.title: Trump pursues last-ditch hunt for voter fraud
33e1d7779a:06796907bdd618ee.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:06796907bdd618ee.summary: The Trump administration says Americans should prepare between now and Election Day for a wave of new arrests and prosecutions over alleged non-citizen voter fraud . Why it matters: The Trump administration is deploying hundreds of federal investigators and attorneys to pursue President Trump's long-running fixation — and test a broader Republican claim that tougher enforcement will uncover far more illegal voting. "This initiative is a tier one priority," a Justice Department official told reporters on Tuesday. "It's a top priority for the attorney general and for the White House." The big picture: Across the country, there are now 1,600 open cases of potential voter fraud and 160 people have been arrested, a Homeland Security Investigations official said Tuesday. HSI agents have been requesting and combing through publicly available voter data to find cases of non-citizens registering to vote or voting when they're ineligible. The FBI has been working on these cases too. DOJ has charged 24 immigrants this calendar year following the prioritization, according to agency press releases. The accused are a mixture of undocumented immigrations and legal residents. The number of prosecutions will "rise significantly each week going forward from now until the election," the DOJ official said. Zoom in: To support these investigations, which the HSI official called agent-time intensive, Homeland Security staff have shifted work time from other priorities. HSI agents typically investigate smuggling, trafficking, financial fraud and sexual exploitation crimes. The intrigue: Staff usually focused on finding immigration fraud at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the office for legal immigration, have also been tasked with searching for possible non-citizens registered in state voter files. This staff sent referrals to HSI to investigate, according to the New York Times , and flagged the potential non-citizens by the thousands to state election officials . For three…

33e1d7779a:be434ea1d4460d25.title: The All-In-ification of Trump's AI agenda
33e1d7779a:be434ea1d4460d25.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:be434ea1d4460d25.summary: President Trump's accelerationist AI doctrine increasingly bears the stamp of the "All-In" podcast, whose tech-investor network now feeds ideas and talent directly into the White House. Why it matters: An unlikely marriage of convenience between MAGA and Silicon Valley has proved remarkably durable, deepening as Trump sheds support elsewhere and stakes more of his legacy on dominating the AI race. Zoom in: No figure has done more to bridge the two worlds than David Sacks , the "All-In" co-host who spent Trump's first year as his AI czar and remains a powerful outside adviser with direct access to the president. Sacks helped build Trump's original AI agenda around a simple premise: move fast, sweep away regulatory barriers and treat China — not catastrophic risk — as the overriding threat. Anthropic's highly capable Mythos model posed the first serious challenge to that doctrine in May, rattling the White House enough to consider pre-release oversight of frontier models. But Trump watered down the 90-day review plan after Sacks and industry leaders warned that three months amounted to an eternity in frontier AI — and could slow U.S. labs as China raced ahead. Zoom out: Sacks left the White House but not Trump's inner circle, shaping AI policy as co-chair of the president's science council while the broader "All-In" network embeds itself deeper across Trumpworld. David Friedberg serves on the same council alongside investor Marc Andreessen, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other tech leaders — putting half of "All-In"'s core cast on the president's formal science-policy panel. Chamath Palihapitiya , another co-host and prominent Trump booster, is among the names being floated for the new AI czar job Trump announced last weekend. Brad Gerstner , a frequent fill-in on the podcast, helped conceive Trump Accounts and became one of the program's chief evangelists. The intrigue: Jason Calacanis, the show's moderator, is the political outlier — frequently criticizing Trump on…

33e1d7779a:eb75a3157063c7eb.title: Uber's robotaxi edge: human drivers
33e1d7779a:eb75a3157063c7eb.author: Joann Muller
33e1d7779a:eb75a3157063c7eb.summary: Uber is betting billions on a driverless future, but the secret to making the economics work could be — surprise! — its vast army of human drivers. Why it matters: Uber believes a hybrid network of robots and people can keep its expensive autonomous vehicles busier, and therefore more profitable, than fleets made up entirely of robotaxis. The big picture: Think of a high-tech robotaxi like an airplane: It costs money whether it's carrying passengers or sitting on the ground. The more trips each vehicle makes, the more revenue Uber and its robotaxi partners can squeeze from that expensive asset, offsetting the fixed costs of the technology, vehicle financing, insurance, depot space and other infrastructure. Between the lines: Ride-hailing is a supply-driven business, and robotaxis aren't a substitute for drivers, Uber says — they're an additional form of supply. With greater supply comes lower prices and shorter wait times, which means increased reliability. That stimulates more demand, and ultimately makes the ride-hailing pie bigger. That's Uber's theory. Robotaxi economics remain unproven , Uber's own president of autonomous mobility and delivery, Sarfraz Maredia, tells Axios. It's still early, and no company is making money yet operating them, nor is anyone yet operating them at massive scale. Whether AVs and all that's needed to support a fleet — including charging infrastructure and maintenance — will ultimately be cheaper than today's ride-hailing model "very much has yet to be proven," Maredia says. "The unit economics today have a long way to go." Uber's bet is that its mix of human drivers and AVs will produce better returns. How it works: In a hybrid network — and Lyft has a similar philosophy —AVs would handle the steady "base load" of everyday demand. Human drivers, meanwhile, would provide extra capacity during rush hour, bad weather, concerts and other demand spikes. Maredia points to late nights as an example: Uber can recharge robotaxis when…

33e1d7779a:111e3881c6c15871.title: Scoop: Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan
33e1d7779a:111e3881c6c15871.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:111e3881c6c15871.summary: President Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday. Why it matters: The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war reconstruction and governance in Gaza would look like. The plan is a result of a year of work by dozens of people both on the Board of Peace, which includes 28 member countries, and in the Palestinian technocratic government. It includes projected spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, according to a copy of the plan obtained by Axios. "The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster," a Board of Peace official said. Yes, but: For the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate. While the Netanyahu government has agreed in principle to aspects of the plan that have been previously discussed, it refused to start implementing it , mainly for domestic political reasons ahead of the elections. And while Hamas agreed in principle to disarm , it hasn't been tested yet, partly because Israel won't implement a 14-day ceasefire before the demilitarization process starts. The Board of Peace hopes that after the Israeli elections on Oct. 27 and the formation of a new Israeli government, the Gaza recovery process can finally start. But the election is unlikely to yield a clear winner, resulting in a caretaker government and a political stalemate. That could further undermine implementation of the Gaza proposal. The big picture: The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade. Zoom in: The plan divides the 66 projects into six areas: infrastructure development, human development, economic acceleration, digital…

33e1d7779a:5320fa55636f03bf.title: Poll: Americans see rule of law declining in U.S.
33e1d7779a:5320fa55636f03bf.author: Margaret Talev
33e1d7779a:5320fa55636f03bf.summary: Data: Charles F. Kettering Foundation and Gallup; Note: Values shown may not total 100% due to rounding and exclusion of "don't know" responses; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Visuals A majority of Americans say the rule of law in the U.S. is weaker now than a decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected president, according to a massive new survey of more than 23,000 U.S. adults. Driving the news: 78% of those responding to the survey by Gallup and the Charles F. Kettering Foundation for its Democracy for All Project say government officials must always follow laws and the Constitution. But just 28% trust that political leaders will be held accountable if they don't. Zoom in: Throwing out incumbents was respondents' top choice (17%) when asked what one step could be taken to most improve U.S. democracy. That response reflects a prominent theme of a midterm campaign that's shadowed by widespread voter dissatisfaction. Other steps suggested by survey respondents included electoral reform and improved voting access (13%) and limiting executive power (9%). One stunning stat: Older Republicans (65+) appear significantly less trusting of election officials now than just a year ago, with 42% saying it's reasonable to assume that election officials acted improperly if election outcomes are surprising, up from 30%. By the numbers: The share of Americans who say the rule of law is weaker now than in 2016 is four times higher than the share who think it's stronger (56% compared with 14%), while 29% say it's unchanged. Democrats and independents were much likelier than Republicans to say it's weaker. The top reason respondents cited for getting involved in a social or political cause: Feeling an important right or freedom is being threatened (27%), followed by feeling you can make a difference (26%) and seeing officials abuse or misuse power (19%). 57% said they prefer candidates who challenge powerful or established interests, while 42% prefer candidates who work within the…

33e1d7779a:fa8e5e38733e9757.title: AI labs are cutting model costs - and it could help them slow down safely
33e1d7779a:fa8e5e38733e9757.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:fa8e5e38733e9757.summary: The shift of the AI frontier toward more powerful, lower-cost models could pave the way for safely slowing development, experts say. Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development. Otherwise financial incentives will be too powerful . Driving the news : The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will be for the foreseeable future. Their top executives have also shown unusual solidarity in expressing a desire to slow the pace of model development due to a troubling series of incidents in which rogue AI agents hacked outside companies. Between the lines : To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable. That's because remaining at the so-called frontier of capabilities requires a treadmill of never-ending — and mind-boggling spending — to keep up. Slowing the extent of that spending, some of which is used for the computing firepower needed to train new models, would help the companies generate better returns. That wouldn't necessarily threaten spending on computing, data centers and infrastructure such as upgrading the electric grid, according to some economists and AI pros. Those investments will still be needed in order to service demand for AI usage that continues to skyrocket. Catch up quick: Everybody gets a new model this week, and the one thing they all have in common is that they're cheaper than ever without forgoing top intelligence. OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX all emphasized the relatively low costs of their new models this week, as well as their ability to outperform some of their own top systems from only a few months ago. Chinese models including DeepSeek have done the…

33e1d7779a:b23b5b42feeb41b0.title: FBI investigating claims that a major cybercrime group stole sensitive personnel data
33e1d7779a:b23b5b42feeb41b0.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:b23b5b42feeb41b0.summary: A notorious cybercrime group is claiming they stole more than 2 terabytes of data that includes detailed personal information about thousands of FBI employees and job applicants. Why it matters : Cybercriminals and state-sponsored attackers have penetrated U.S. IT systems for years, but stealing detailed and sensitive information about FBI employees is brazen, cyber experts told Axios. Cybercriminals are known to trade leaked information on the dark web, a prospect that would leave the data up for grabs from the highest bidder. Driving the news : ShinyHunters, a group that's broken into numerous institutions, said in a post on its dark-web site Tuesday that it stole "very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job." An FBI spokesperson said in a statement the bureau is "aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating." What to watch : Cynthia Kaiser, a former top official in the FBI's cyber division, told Axios that when a hacker targets the FBI, expect the bureau "to marshal additional resources to bring them more quickly to justice." The big picture : While the breach is likely to bring more law enforcement attention to ShinyHunters in the short term, the long tail impact is greater on the FBI employees and their families whose information was stolen, Allan Liska, a threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, told Axios. "The data is out there and has likely been repeatedly downloaded and passed around to other threat actors," Liska said. Axios has not been able to corroborate that the data stolen is legitimate or recent, but cybersecurity researchers confirmed that the attack appears legitimate. 404 Media obtained a sample of the stolen data, which appears to include information about 5,000 alleged agents. Zoom in : ShinyHunters told Axios in an email that the stolen data includes names, FBI agent statuses, emails, phone numbers, home addresses…

33e1d7779a:1906702651d891db.title: GOP breaking with an unpopular Trump
33e1d7779a:1906702651d891db.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:1906702651d891db.summary: Congressional Republicans are increasingly breaking with an unpopular president on foreign policy and pocketbook issues as they try to stop their majorities from slipping away. Why it matters: They aren't engaged in a full-scale revolt against President Trump, but some Republicans are testing new ways to distance themselves from him — a sign of their election anxiety. Driving the news: Trump — facing a barrage of demands from Republican lawmakers to impose a ban on diesel exports — pulled a rare about-face Tuesday, saying on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that he'll support a ban. Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), along with Iowa GOP Reps. Ashley Hinson and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, were among those calling for a ban to ease skyrocketing diesel costs for U.S. farmers and truckers. Sullivan and Hinson are in tight Senate races. Just on Tuesday: Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) railed on the Senate floor at Trump's decision to host Chinese President Xi Jinping this week for a state dinner. Wicker urged Trump to "keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly" at the U.S. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) called for the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. over his foreign business dealings and the hundreds of thousands of dollars he allegedly received from a Russian oligarch for his wedding. "If your family's involved in the [presidency], then you ought to be very transparent," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a close Trump ally, told Axios last week when asked about the reporting on Trump Jr.'s wedding. On Iran: The Senate is expected to vote this week on a war powers resolution. Leadership can't guarantee it won't get the Republican votes needed to pass. "We're constantly, of course, checking," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "But I would hope that you know the team could hang…

33e1d7779a:4fe2f9a32f90ed2f.title: Trump TV is live. Here's what it's actually showing
33e1d7779a:4fe2f9a32f90ed2f.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:4fe2f9a32f90ed2f.summary: As President Trump fights the press over coverage, the White House launched its own 24/7 streaming channel — Trump TV. Why it matters: Trump TV gives the president a White House-run video platform to reach the public without relying on traditional news organizations. So far, Trump TV resembles a round-the-clock presidential highlight reel more than a news network. Driving the news: Trump TV launched the same day major TV networks suspended White House pool coverage — a protest that left one Trump speech airing without sound. The White House had teased the channel through cryptic videos , and it went live on its YouTube account, WhiteHouse.gov and the official White House app. Reality check: Presidents have long used White House platforms to share speeches and events with the public. What we know about Trump TV How it works: The channel launched as "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station." "Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration's greatest hits, unfiltered," Kaelan Dorr, deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X . So far, the channel has shown curated clips of past Trump speeches and executive actions, along with live events. Catch up quick: The initial programming included Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech before shifting into footage of his 2025 inauguration, per multiple reports . The Daily Beast reports 8,500 viewers were watching the stream during its first hour. Around 1,200 people were watching Tuesday afternoon as the channel aired a Trump health care announcement from August, according to an Axios review of the stream. Zoom in: The stream can also carry live events. On Tuesday, the stream carried Vice President Vance's briefing on fraud claims. But while Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday morning, Trump TV was replaying an earlier speech from the National Prayer Breakfast. Unanswered questions about Trump TV What we're watching: So far, Trump TV has no anchors, news ticker or headline chyrons. The stream includes…

33e1d7779a:36900cf93f1d5859.title: Trump backs ban on diesel exports
33e1d7779a:36900cf93f1d5859.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:36900cf93f1d5859.summary: President Trump said during a Tuesday press interview alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that he has also 'called for' a ban on U.S. diesel exports, joining other conservative voices who endorse the policy. Why it matters: Trump's endorsement marks a shift for an administration that has resisted calls to restrict fuel exports, as record diesel prices squeeze farmers and truckers and fuel Republican concerns ahead of the midterms . Economists and energy analysts say the move could benefit America in the short term but would likely raise prices globally, including in the U.S. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:5f3dc07649373148.title: Cheap, powerful AI models are increasing usage, a bullish sign for the AI boom
33e1d7779a:5f3dc07649373148.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:5f3dc07649373148.summary: AI companies have competed on having the best and often most dangerous models for years. Now, they're pivoting to a new focus: cost. Why it matters: The biggest risk to the AI boom is demand, and recent innovations to make models cheaper while maintaining powerful levels of intelligence have offered a bullish signal. As the prices of top models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others come down, usage is increasing dramatically, a trend that points to the kind of demand that will be necessary to justify trillions of dollars in spending. State of play: It's modelpalooza in the AI world this week, with OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and some Chinese model providers all offering new releases. Most of them are offering shocking levels of intelligence at prices that would've been unthinkable just a few months ago. OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Tuesday, which brings down the cost for top business customers by 50% from previous iterations of the same models, the company shared with Axios. Anthropic is releasing Opus 5.5 on Tuesday, which the company says costs around 40% less to run than Opus 5 while maintaining top intelligence. Elon Musk's xAI on Monday released Grok 4.7 , pitching the new model around price-performance. Yet in a testament to the sheer brutality of competition in the AI race, it only took 24 hours for new options to wipe out much of that price advantage. Threat level: The ferocity and speed of the race during an ongoing price war is an issue for OpenAI and Anthropic, which need to retain customers and revenue growth to justify their sky-high multi-trillion-dollar valuations. Yes, but : Even as they face margin pressure, the trend is positive for the AI boom overall, as the price reductions make it much easier to bet on a bright future for AI use. Follow the money: There is emerging evidence that cost cutting is a rising tide that can lift revenues for all AI providers. In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token…

33e1d7779a:c1e57b454fd6edc1.title: Exclusive: Trump adviser ties high gas prices to refining
33e1d7779a:c1e57b454fd6edc1.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:c1e57b454fd6edc1.summary: The affordability of gasoline remains "the top issue that the president looks at," Trump energy adviser Jarrod Agen said at an Axios House event Tuesday. Why it matters: The Trump administration is championing energy savings from its deregulatory push as overseas conflicts, including the Iran war, rattle oil markets, driving up fuel costs and threatening an expensive winter for millions of households. Tuesday's national average gas price was roughly $4.48, up from around $3.18 a year ago, per AAA . Driving the news: Asked by Axios' Amy Harder if the president takes responsibility for the higher prices Americans are paying, Agen said that the president's "long-term goal is preventing Iran" from having "nuclear capabilities." "He says the long term is worth it to stop them from having a nuclear weapon." Flashback: Asked last year what a successful term would look like once the administration's time in Washington is up, Agen told Axios' Mike Allen that the one factor the president always looks at is the price at the pump. "We want to make sure that U.S. consumers are paying not high prices on their electricity bills and gas," he said. "That is the key that ... drives us every single day." Zoom in: Pressed on those remarks, Agen told Harder it's "still the top issue the president looks at" and attributed the price pain to strained refining capacity. "We've got crude flowing," he said, though the full picture of how much oil is leaving the Strait of Hormuz isn't yet entirely clear . "More crude is on the market, and so that's great. But refining capacity is the issue we're trying to solve, both domestically and then globally," Agen said. "If you look at refining capacity, Russia, for example, it's down 30, 40% China is not at their capacity." He floated the possibility of relief via the Defense Production Act, which Trump already invoked , and infrastructure projects "to attack the refining issue." Catch up quick: The national average diesel price shattered its record…

33e1d7779a:9a8be53dbccc7de7.title: Arab mediators push for U.S.-Iran meeting at U.N. to de-escalate crisis
33e1d7779a:9a8be53dbccc7de7.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:9a8be53dbccc7de7.summary: Several Arab countries mediating between the U.S. and Iran are in contact with both sides about arranging a high-level meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, according to a regional source involved in the talks. Why it matters: The gathering in New York offers Gulf countries a rare opportunity to try to break the stalemate in the war, which is approaching the seven-month mark with no signs of a breakthrough. State of play: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC Tuesday that President Trump is open to meeting with the Iranians in New York "because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems." He added, however, that no meeting has been scheduled yet. Trump is expected to meet with representatives of nine Arab countries on Tuesday to discuss the war. Many of the countries are expected to urge Trump to de-escalate with Iran and work to reach a deal, regional sources said. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Tuesday morning in New York with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who is a key mediator between Iran and the U.S. What he said: In his speech before the UN General Assembly, Trump reiterated what he told Axios last week: that he has "a big decision to make" whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilating the Islamic Republic." Trump said he thinks the U.S. will reach a deal with Iran after the midterms "We will get it done one way or another. We will get it done and get it done fast," Trump said. "It doesn't make sense for Iran not to (make a deal)," he added. "They are waiting to see how I do in the midterm elections. What they don't realize is that I am not running … I will be here for two-and-a-half years. I gave no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran.
